sections.section_title: Foundations: Severe Aortic Stenosis, TAVI Durability, and the Challenge of Serial Redo Procedures
sections.description: This section introduces the focused background needed to understand the case: why TAVI is used, how transcatheter valves fail over time, how prior endocarditis complicates interpretation, and why a third transcatheter valve is anatomically and hemodynamically difficult.
subtopics: Hemodynamic consequences of severe aortic stenosis and the rationale for valve replacement
How TAVI became an established therapy across surgical risk groups
Key transcatheter valve design features relevant to this case: Lotus, Evolut, and Acurate neo2
Mechanisms of transcatheter bioprosthetic valve failure: structural degeneration, leaflet fibrosis, calcification, malexpansion, and mixed stenosis-regurgitation
Redo transcatheter strategies: TAV-in-TAV and the rarer TAV-in-TAV-in-TAV configuration
Why layered valve frames reduce effective orifice area and increase the risk of prosthesis-patient mismatch
Coronary obstruction, neo-skirt formation, commissural misalignment, and loss of future coronary access in serial valve interventions
Prosthetic valve endocarditis after TAVI: how active infection differs from healed infection in diagnosis and treatment planning
How endocarditis can contribute to later leaflet injury, restriction, and accelerated prosthetic dysfunction
The concept of lifetime management in structural valve disease, including planning for future reinterventions from the first TAVI onward

sections.section_title: Clinical Course: From First TAVI to Post-Endocarditis Failure of Two Prior Prostheses
sections.description: This section reconstructs the patient's longitudinal history and shows how comorbidity burden, repeated prior interventions, and treated prosthetic valve endocarditis set the stage for consideration of a third valve procedure.
subtopics: Baseline patient profile and symptom presentation: exertional dyspnoea, chest discomfort, dizziness, and fatigue
Comorbidities shaping risk and management: hypertension, multivessel coronary artery disease, prior PCI, pacemaker for complete AV block, diabetes, COPD, and recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding
Initial 2014 TAVI with a 27 mm Lotus valve for severe aortic stenosis
Clinical and echocardiographic progression to degeneration of the first transcatheter valve by 2021-2022
Evidence of severe prosthetic stenosis before the second intervention: rising gradients and decline in left ventricular ejection fraction
2022 TAV-in-TAV with implantation of a 23 mm Evolut valve
Postprocedural vascular complication after the second TAVI: femoral haematoma and pseudoaneurysm requiring open repair
Early hemodynamic benefit after the second TAVI and recovery of left ventricular function
September 2022 prosthetic valve endocarditis: fever, worsening heart failure, severe restenosis, and Enterococcus faecalis bacteremia
Antimicrobial treatment course for prosthetic valve endocarditis and interval clinical improvement
2024 recurrence of severe prosthetic dysfunction with both high gradient and moderate-to-severe intraprosthetic regurgitation across two overlapping valves

sections.section_title: Preprocedural Evaluation: Defining Valve Failure, Excluding Active Infection, and Determining Feasibility
sections.description: This section explains the diagnostic workup and clinical reasoning that moved the team from symptom recurrence to a decision for a third transcatheter intervention. It emphasizes echocardiography, CT planning, infection reassessment, differential diagnosis, and surgical-risk analysis.
subtopics: The core clinical questions before reintervention: What is failing, why is it failing, is infection still active, and is another catheter-based procedure feasible?

Transthoracic echocardiographic assessment of prosthetic valve dysfunction: mean gradient, aortic valve area, indexed aortic valve area, Doppler velocity index, regurgitation severity, and ejection fraction
Use of the continuity equation to calculate aortic valve area in prosthetic aortic valves
How to interpret severe mixed prosthetic stenosis and regurgitation in a patient with multiple prior valve frames
Transoesophageal echocardiography to exclude vegetations, abscess, paravalvular complications, and other signs of active prosthetic valve endocarditis
Microbiologic reassessment: repeated blood cultures and criteria supporting resolved rather than ongoing infection

Multislice CT measurements relevant to a third TAVI: minimum lumen diameter, coronary ostial height, sinus of Valsalva dimensions, valve-to-coronary distance, frame interaction, and anticipated neo-skirt position
Why a minimum lumen diameter of 13.7 mm signaled severe hemodynamic compromise but still allowed procedural planning

Differential diagnosis of recurrent high prosthetic gradients: structural degeneration, infection-related leaflet injury, thrombosis, underexpansion, and pre-existing or acquired prosthesis-patient mismatch
Assessment of prohibitive surgical risk: EuroSCORE II, comorbidity burden, prior valve integration into the aortic wall, and the likely need for complex root and ascending aorta surgery
Guideline context: why surgery is generally preferred in prosthetic valve endocarditis, and why individualized management is appropriate after infection has been eradicated
Multidisciplinary heart-team decision-making as the bridge from diagnostic data to procedural choice

sections.section_title: Intervention: CT-Guided TAV-in-TAV-in-TAV Planning and Execution
sections.description: This section details how the third valve procedure was planned and performed. The emphasis is on device selection, imaging-based strategy, coronary protection logic, implantation depth, commissural alignment, and the technical steps used to optimize hemodynamics in triple-stented anatomy.
subtopics: Procedural goals in a triple-valve anatomy: restore function, avoid coronary obstruction, preserve future coronary access, and maximize residual effective orifice area
Why a self-expanding Acurate neo2 size S was selected for this case
Advantages of supra-annular leaflet position and relatively lower frame height in a narrow, multiply stented aortic root
Institutional approval for off-label use and the role of shared decision-making with the patient and family
Access strategy and anesthetic approach: local anesthesia with radial and femoral arterial access
Baseline aortography to confirm severe aortic regurgitation before valve deployment
Guidewire and catheter strategy, including Safari wire positioning in the left ventricle
Balloon predilation under rapid pacing as both a preparatory maneuver and a real-time test of coronary safety
How preprocedural CT and fluoroscopic planning guided high implantation at the level of the Evolut leaflets
The logic of high implantation: fixing prior leaflets outward, limiting inward folding, reducing neo-skirt below the coronaries, and improving effective orifice area
Commissural alignment as a deliberate strategy to preserve coronary reaccess and reduce future procedural complexity
Why coronary protection or BASILICA was not used in this case despite the theoretical risk
Post-dilation to improve valve expansion, central flow, and leaflet mechanics within the prior frames
Intraoperative endpoints: correct position, preserved coronary perfusion, and absence of transvalvular or paravalvular regurgitation
Complications that must be anticipated in serial TAVI procedures, including coronary obstruction, vascular injury, embolization, residual stenosis, and difficult future coronary access
Application of Valve Academic Research Consortium-3 criteria to define procedural success

sections.section_title: Results, Hemodynamic Interpretation, and Lifetime Management Lessons
sections.description: This section interprets the postprocedural findings, explains the initially high but later improved gradients, reviews the 1-year outcome, and extracts broader lessons about surveillance and long-term planning after repeated transcatheter valve interventions.
subtopics: Immediate postprocedural echocardiography: mobile leaflets, no regurgitation, but high mean gradient and small calculated valve area
Recognition of severe prosthesis-patient mismatch immediately after the third procedure using mean gradient, indexed valve area, and Doppler velocity index
Why an initially high gradient after complex valve-in-valve therapy does not always indicate procedural failure
Mechanisms of later hemodynamic improvement: better frame expansion after post-dilation, improved leaflet opening, altered flow dynamics, and left ventricular remodeling
One-month follow-up: fall in mean gradient, increase in valve area, and stabilization in the moderately stenotic range
Clinical and echocardiographic status at 3.5 months and 1 year: symptom relief, preserved ejection fraction, no recurrent regurgitation, and no recurrent endocarditis
How to structure follow-up after TAV-in-TAV-in-TAV: serial echocardiography, symptom review, infection surveillance, and planning around future coronary access
What this case suggests about transcatheter reintervention after treated prosthetic valve endocarditis when surgery is prohibitive

Limits of future rescue options if the third prosthesis fails: technically hazardous explantation, uncertain role of valve fracture, and possible but unproven leaflet-laceration strategies in triple-stented anatomy
Key teaching points for trainees: anatomy-driven decision-making, CT-based procedural planning, heart-team judgment, and lifetime strategy in structural valve disease
